opus-5.5.text:
I think it's plausible, though I'd frame it a bit differently than people often do. The cost of a robot isn't really set by the motors and the metal. A lot of it comes from the fact that, historically, robots have had to be extremely precise, extremely stiff, and extremely repeatable, because the software controlling them was fairly dumb. If your control system just replays a trajectory, the hardware has to land in exactly the same place every time, and that precision is expensive.

Once you have learned controllers that look at the world, notice they're a centimeter off, and correct, you can relax many of those requirements. You can use cheaper actuators, more backlash, less rigid materials, and let the intelligence compensate. We've already seen this in research. Some of the arms people use for learning-based manipulation now cost a small fraction of what an industrial arm costs, and they can do surprisingly dexterous things because the policy fills the gap.

So I think the trend line is real. The other big factor is scale. Right now robots are built in tiny volumes, nearly hand-assembled. If there's real demand, because the robots are actually useful in homes, warehouses, and kitchens, manufacturing economics kick in the way they did for phones, drones, or cars. A drone with cameras, compute, motors, and a battery costs a few hundred dollars today, and that wasn't obvious twenty years ago.

That said, I'd be careful about the timeline. Hardware cost isn't the main bottleneck in my view. The bottleneck is whether the robot can do something useful enough to justify buying it. If the foundation models get good enough that a cheap arm on a mobile base can reliably do chores or handle varied tasks, the market will pull the costs down. If they don't, nobody will build a million of them, and they'll stay expensive. Whether we hit hundreds of dollars by the end of the decade depends mostly on how fast the learning side progresses, and I'm fairly optimistic about that, but it's the variable that matters.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls lower costs plausible and discusses cost drivers, but does not state that robot cost declines have repeatedly exceeded Sergey Levine’s expectations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's very plausible, and honestly I think the hardware question is less of a bottleneck than people assume. If you look at what's actually in a robotic arm, it's motors, gearboxes, some structural components, and a bit of electronics. None of that is exotic. The reason arms have historically cost tens of thousands of dollars is that they were built for industrial settings where you need very high precision, very high repeatability, very high payload, and where the volume was small so there was no pressure to drive costs down.

What changes the equation is learning. If the robot is controlled by a learned policy that's using cameras and feedback from the environment, you don't actually need the arm to be precise to a fraction of a millimeter in open loop. You can have a cheaper arm with more backlash, more compliance, less accurate encoders, and the policy just compensates, the same way your own arm is not a precision instrument but you can still thread a needle because you're closing the loop with your eyes. So learning essentially lets you trade off expensive hardware for software, and software is the thing that gets cheap at scale.

We already see hints of this. There are hobbyist-grade arms in the low hundreds of dollars range that people in the research community use for data collection and for running policies, and they work surprisingly well for a lot of tasks. They're not going to lift a car engine, but for manipulating household objects they're adequate. The mobile base adds some cost, but again, the components there, wheels, batteries, motors, are commodity parts.

The caveat I'd add is that the price of the hardware only matters once the capability is there. Nobody cares if an arm costs three hundred dollars if it can't do anything useful. So the real question is whether, by the end of the decade, we have the models that make a cheap, imprecise robot genuinely useful in an unstructured environment. I'm optimistic about that, but that's the harder part, and if we get it right then the economics will follow pretty quickly, because once there's demand at consumer scale, manufacturing costs come down the way they did for phones or drones.

r001.rationale: The candidate says low-cost robotic arms are plausible and discusses why costs may fall, but it does not say that robot cost declines have repeatedly exceeded Sergey Levine’s expectations.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s plausible, but I would distinguish the cost of the hardware from the cost of a system that can actually do useful things reliably. You can build a fairly inexpensive arm if you’re willing to compromise on precision, payload, and durability. Whether that’s the arm you want working in your kitchen every day is a different question.

One of the exciting possibilities with learning is that we might be able to compensate for some of those hardware limitations. If your control system can adapt to imperfect actuators, or use vision to correct errors, then you don’t necessarily need the same precision engineering you would need for a robot executing a fixed trajectory in a factory.

But there’s also a volume question. Robots are expensive partly because we don’t make very many of them. If we can get to the point where a cheap mobile manipulator does something people actually want, that creates demand, which makes it worthwhile to manufacture at scale. So I wouldn’t rule out hundreds of dollars by the end of the decade. I’m more uncertain about what that robot will be capable of doing, and how much human intervention it will need.

r001.rationale: The candidate says costs could reach hundreds of dollars, but does not state that robot cost declines have repeatedly exceeded Sergey Levine’s expectations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s plausible, though it depends on what you mean by a mobile robotic arm. A system that moves around and picks up relatively light objects is a different proposition from something that can do everything a person can do with their hands.

The interesting question is how much of the cost today is actually necessary, and how much comes from building small numbers of robots for customers who need very precise, reliable hardware. If you have good feedback and good learned control, you can potentially tolerate much cheaper hardware. You don’t necessarily need every component to be precise if the system can observe what happened and correct for it.

But software doesn’t make the physical constraints disappear. Motors have to produce enough torque, gears have to survive wear, and batteries have to supply enough energy. So I wouldn’t confidently predict a broadly capable household robot for hundreds of dollars by the end of the decade. A useful, relatively limited mobile manipulator at that price seems much more conceivable. And then the question is whether its capabilities are useful enough to create the volume that brings the price down further.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a limited mobile manipulator at that price seems conceivable, but does not state that robot cost declines have repeatedly exceeded Levine’s expectations.
